title: A Flavour Made of Weather
logline: For six or seven weeks a year a hot dry wind crosses one hill district, the rain stops, and the taste of the only crop grown there changes enough that buyers on the other side of the world pay more for it; the film watches a whole district's work organised around a flavour that is not kept anywhere.
human_question: If the taste I am paying for is made by a wind that will stop next month, where exactly is it being kept until then?

place.what_kind_of_place: Steep, east-facing hill country in which nearly every acre for twenty kilometres in any direction is under one crop. It is worked in blocks by hand, picked twice a day, and carried within hours to small factories that then run all night. For six or seven weeks each year a hot dry wind comes over the ridge from the far side of the island, the rain stops, the days are hot and the nights cold, and the bushes are stressed enough that the leaf they make tastes different from the leaf they made in June. Nothing else about the place changes for those weeks: the same slopes, the same hands, the same hundred-year-old machinery. Only the weather, and what the weather does to a taste, and what people will pay for it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off. The wind is visible: it crosses the slope as a moving wave through waist-high bush, and from directly above, the whole hillside changes colour as it passes and changes back behind it. Cloud comes over the ridge in the early morning and pours down the eastern face like something spilled, then burns off in minutes, so the same valley is white, then green, then white again. And inside the factory there is a long bench in flat daylight with two rows of identical white cups on it, the liquor bright, steam standing off them, and a spoon going down the row faster than looks possible.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Everything runs on a clock nobody in the film sets. The wind gets up late in the morning and drops at dusk. Leaf has to reach the factory the same day it is taken off the bush. The withering runs through the night in a building with the doors open and fans on, and the smell in it changes hour by hour as the firing starts. Across the six weeks the colour in the cups changes, and so does the number written beside them. Then the wind stops and the place goes back to being ordinary, at ordinary prices, without anything visible having happened.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry-wind weeks, roughly July into early September, which is the only window in which the film exists at all. Early morning for cloud on the eastern face and for the first leaf of the day; late afternoon for the wind at full strength and for low light raking the slope. The tasting bench wants flat north daylight, which is when it is genuinely used, so no light has to be brought in for it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A weather film about a hillside and a crop. It has a complete shape of its own: a wind arrives, everything sharpens and speeds up, a season is made out of six weeks, the wind goes. A viewer who never hears a word of the narration gets cloud pouring over a ridge, a visible wind, night work in a hot building, a smell they can nearly taste, and one very beautiful bench of cups in daylight at the end of it.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' account of feeling, performed at district scale by people who have never heard of it. The voice never contradicts the picture and never suggests that anybody's trade or pleasure is a mistake; it points at what is already on screen. A famous, expensive flavour turns out to be made of weather. The mouth that knows it best registers the least. Bodies ache while the people they belong to laugh. And when the wind stops, the flavour goes, although the hill, the bush and the leaf are exactly what they were.

sequence.on_screen: First light from the air. A single crop running over every ridge and hollow to the skyline, cloud lying in the valleys below, one thread of smoke from a factory chimney.
sequence.voice: Everything you can see was planted because of a taste. Not a staple, not a medicine, not anything anybody needs: a taste. The old compendiums this series reads have a name for the world that runs on things like this. The everyday world, the one made of what is seen and heard and smelled and tasted and touched. They do not dismiss it. They count it.

sequence.on_screen: Late morning. From directly above, a wave of movement crossing the bushes, the colour of the slope changing as it goes and changing back behind it. Dust lifting off a track.
sequence.voice: This is the thing the buyers are paying for, and you can watch it arrive. For six weeks a dry wind comes over that ridge, the rain stops, and the bush makes a leaf that tastes different. The books have a word for what happens when that leaf finally meets somebody, and the word they use is tasting. Feeling, they say, is the tasting of the flavour of whatever is in front of the mind, and it is in every mind, because there is always something in front of it.

sequence.on_screen: The pluck. Hands moving faster than the eye at waist height, heat, a sack filling on someone's back, insects. Then the afternoon weigh-in: the hook, the tally, and a good deal of talk and laughing in the queue.
sequence.voice: Two different things are being felt here and the books count them separately. What the body is getting, which they give one seat only, touch. And what the mind is doing on top of it, which is a separate item altogether. A back can be hurting while the person it belongs to is laughing in the queue. That is not bravery and it is not pretence. It is two feelings, in two places, at the same time.

sequence.on_screen: Night in the factory. Withering troughs a hundred feet long, fans, the floor above lit and the floor below dark, leaf going into the rollers, the smell of the firing changing as the hours pass.
sequence.voice: Nothing arrives without a taste on it. Pleasant, unpleasant, or neither, and the sources are firm that there is no fourth way of getting anything at all. Neither is not an absence. It has its own name in their list, and by their own count almost as many moments carry it as carry gladness. Most of this night is being lived in it.

sequence.on_screen: The tasting bench in flat daylight. Two rows of identical white cups, the liquor poured, the leaf beside each one. A spoon goes down the row, a mouth draws and spits, a number is written. No expression at any point.
sequence.voice: That is the mouth in this district that knows the taste best, and it is the one getting least out of it. The books help here, in a way that is almost a relief. Wanting, they say, arrives either with gladness or with nothing much at all, and never with displeasure. So a flat face proves nothing about the cup, and a delighted face proves nothing either. Both are accurate reports of the same liquid.

sequence.on_screen: Sacks graded, stencilled and stacked; a figure written on a board; a phone call taken in the yard with the wind still moving the trees behind the speaker.
sequence.voice: A price is being set on weather, and nobody here pretends otherwise. They will tell you which fields caught the wind this week and which sat in the lee of a hill and missed it. What is being sold is not sitting in the leaf, and it is not sitting in anybody's mouth either. It is what happens when one meets the other, this month, in this wind, and not in June.

sequence.on_screen: The wind has stopped. A still hillside in ordinary weather, cloud back in the valley, ordinary leaf going up the belt, the bench empty and the cups upside down on a cloth.
sequence.voice: Then it stops. The hill is the same hill. The bush is the same bush. The flavour is gone until next year, and nothing you can point at has changed. The books are blunt about that: whatever feels good is standing on conditions, and it hurts when they move. It is not a verdict against pleasure. In their own count of this everyday world, twenty-four of the fifty-four kinds of moment they list are called beautiful. And the tidy line, that pleasure is where wanting begins, is ours. It is not a sentence in these books.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, C032 is not a theory of emotion and not a mood. It is a compendium of one factor: feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, and it is in every mind because every mind has an object [C032-P:L43]. It is threefold by the way it is undergone, with no fourth way, and fivefold as a faculty, and that second list is where the film's spine is, because bodily pleasure and bodily pain get one seat only, touch, while gladness and distress are counted elsewhere [C032-P:L95–L97] [C032-P:L103] [C032-M:L5]. Its last movement is the sober one: conditioned feeling carries a cost because it rests on conditions and hurts when they turn [C032-P:L117], and much of what people undergo is concealed and unknowable without asking [C032-P:L119]. C004 supplies the world this happens in and the caution that keeps the film honest. Sight, smell and taste together are the everyday sense-sphere world the sources count [C004-P:L25]; the count is fifty-four, of which only twelve are unwholesome and twenty-four are called beautiful [C004-P:L27] [C004-P:L31]; and the Margaya's two flat statements do the work at the tasting bench: wanting never comes with displeasure [C004-M:L15], and the same object is met with gladness by one person and with nothing much by another [C004-M:L17]. A district whose entire year turns on a flavour that a wind makes and unmakes is where both can be filmed instead of asserted.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the flavour everyone in the trade can name, grade and price is not being stored anywhere. It is what happens when a particular leaf, made by a particular six weeks of weather, meets a particular person. C032 on its own would make a lecture about feeling. C004 on its own would make a film about desire and shopping. Together they produce a picture in which delight and flatness are both correct, a body's discomfort and a mind's gladness are two separate readings taken at the same moment, and the most valuable thing on the hillside is made of weather and goes when the weather does. The pairing also blocks the group's easiest ending. The sources do not say pleasure is the enemy: the same feeling runs through generous and concentrated minds, and the causal line from pleasure to craving is not in these extracts at all.

concept_links.why: The digest's core sentence is filmable here without staging anything: feeling is the tasting of the flavour of an object, present in every mind because every mind takes an object [C032-P:L43]. The faculty list gives the film its second and third beats, because bodily pleasure and bodily pain have a single seat in touch while gladness is counted separately and far more widely [C032-P:L95–L97] [C032-P:L103] [C032-M:L5], which is why a pluck in the heat and a loud, laughing weigh-in can sit in the same sequence without irony. The seventh beat rests on the suffering of change, where pleasant feeling is counted as costly precisely because it is conditioned and turns [C032-P:L117]. Four guards from the digest are load-bearing and are written into the beats rather than left in the risks. The film must not preach 'chase good vibes', since the sources count even pleasant feeling as conditioned. It must not treat neutral feeling as numbness, because neutral runs through the most refined minds as well as the dullest. It must not present the group's own line, that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins, as source teaching, because the digest says plainly that this is editorial compression and the causal link lies outside these extracts. And it must not let the threefold suffering read as pessimism. The digest also notes that the three kinds of suffering rest on the Pradeepika alone, which is why the voice attributes them as a reading rather than as the doctrine of the tradition.

C004 gives the film both its world and its refusal to accuse anyone. Sight, smell and taste together make up the ordinary sense-sphere world the sources count [C004-P:L25], and this district is that world with one crop in it. The Margaya's definition of the attaching that takes things to be good, beautiful or sweet [C004-M:L13] is what a price list is made of, but the two lines the film actually needs are the ones about feeling: wanting never arrives with displeasure [C004-M:L15], and the same object meets gladness in one person and nothing much in another [C004-M:L17]. That is the tasting bench exactly, and it is what stops the film from reading the taster as jaded or the buyer as greedy. Three of the digest's limits bear directly. 'The sense world is a trap' is ruled out by the sources' own count, in which twenty-four of the fifty-four everyday minds are called beautiful [C004-P:L27]. 'Follow your joy' is ruled out, since joy attends greed-rooted minds as readily as good ones. And the Pradeepika's own moral commentary on trades and pleasures is the author's argument rather than the core of the count, so no line of it is narrated over anybody working here.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a taste is not stored inside the thing you buy. It happens when something arrives in front of somebody, and it depends on conditions that can stop. The proof needs no belief and no vocabulary: a wind crosses a hillside for six weeks, a flavour exists and is paid for, the wind stops, and the flavour is gone while the field, the bush and the leaf stay exactly as they were.
what_must_be_real: The actual working hours of the pluck, the factory and the bench, and the trade's own words for the season, the fields and the liquor. No cup is poured for the camera, no batch is re-tasted for a better shot, no light is brought into the tasting room, and nobody is asked to look delighted or unimpressed. Wages, piece rates and the conditions of the work are shown as they are or not at all, and nobody is asked to describe their day in the film's terms. The wind is filmed on the days it actually blows; it is never simulated and the grade is never pushed to make a season look better than it was.
position_hint: middle: the group's feeling beat, where the film stops asking why people reach and looks instead at the taste that arrives with everything. It wants the group's simpler films about reaching behind it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Romanticising estate labour. The digest names this risk on its own tea seed, and it is the largest risk in the film: this is hard, low-paid, mostly female work, and if the conditions and the pay cannot be shown honestly then the pluck is not used as scenery.
Letting the film become a tea-industry film, with grades, auction prices and export history taking over from the concept.
Presenting the group's line that pleasant feeling is where wanting begins as source teaching; the digest is explicit that it is an editorial compression and beat 7 exists to say so.
Reading feelings off faces and calling the reading doctrine. The film can show a flat mouth and a laughing queue; it cannot announce what anybody is feeling.
Treating neutral feeling as numbness or as a lesser state, which the digest rules out directly.
Letting the threefold suffering land as pessimism, or as a lecture that nobody should enjoy their tea.
Implying that the taster, the buyer or the trade is greedy. The film never calls anybody greedy, and the Pradeepika's own commentary on trades and pleasures stays out of the narration entirely.
The whole payoff depends on a six-week weather window that varies year to year and can fail. A wet season means no film that year.
Consent and power: access is usually granted by a company or a factory manager, not by the people who would be filmed, and their own agreement has to be obtained separately and be revocable.

Overstating the price premium. The auction quotes this district separately in every grade, but the premium is grade-specific and seasonal rather than standing: in one week read directly from a broker's report the district's flavoury leafy grades quoted above the western high growns while its BOP quoted below them, and the region's reported all-time record prices were set in May, outside the quality season. A voice that says buyers simply pay more for this district would be repeating trade lore.

Repeating the popular version of the industry's origin. The commonly told dates — 1867, nineteen acres, twenty-three pounds reaching London in 1873 — differ between the industry's own sources, one of which puts the London valuation in 1881. The narration states what is recorded, names the disagreement, and averages nothing.

Naming the wind wrongly. Trade writing attributes the season to the north-east monsoon or to a wind off the Bay of Bengal; the meteorological definition is a hot dry west or south-west föhn wind belonging to the south-west monsoon, blowing in the lee of the hills. Getting this wrong would also break the film's own argument, which is that the rain on the far side of the ridge is what makes the taste on this side.

Letting the colonial and plantation-labour history in as atmosphere. The estates were cut from land that law presumed to be Crown land, and the district's earlier history includes a rebellion and its suppression. Neither is this film's subject. The history in the voice is that an industry arrived because a crop died and now turns a few weeks of weather into a price; it is recorded and never adjudicated, and it is never mourned — no vanished planting era, no what-they-left-behind.
Letting the historical thread be told for the film by an estate's own heritage presentation, which would turn it into a company history. The dates come from the record, not from a visitor board.
drop_if: Access is offered only on condition that pay, housing and working conditions stay off camera.
The tasting bench can only be filmed as a demonstration staged for visitors rather than as the day's actual work.
The seasonal wind fails, or the season is so poor that the price and the flavour it is built on do not materialise.

connections.note: Two places whose whole economy rests on something that arrives with a season and leaves with it, one a flavour and one a settlement.
A taste that cannot be located in the leaf, and an aim that cannot be located in the movement.

selection.reason: A place where the sources' account of feeling is the working business of the year, with a payoff shot, a visible wind, that states the concept rather than illustrating it.

review.note: Rewritten into the footage-led shape. Dropped the old situation block, which was a household kitchen and a child's first bite, because it was built on people's inner lives and on children in a home. Replaced it with a hill district whose entire year is organised around a flavour that a seasonal wind makes and unmakes, so the concept can be read off the place rather than off a face. New title; old title kept in aliases. Both concept links re-tested against their digests and rewritten: C032 re-grounded on the tasting definition and the separate seats of bodily and mental feeling, with the suffering of change carrying the ending and the editorial 'pleasure is where wanting begins' explicitly refused on screen; C004 kept as the everyday sense world and as the guard that a flat face and a delighted face are both accurate. Added place, two_layers, a seven-beat sequence and a suggested location; the images array is left empty because no candidate image URL could be verified from here. Added 2026-09-26, additively: this record's location and film were not changed and the verdict was already pending, so nothing has been reset. The film's argument and location survived the group's reassignment — hill tea country is a real shooting location and a flavour made of weather and kept nowhere is sound — and what it lacked was history. A full historical_thread has been written: the coffee collapse traced to Thwaites's own record of specimens sent to him from an estate in Madulsima in May 1869 and to Berkeley and Broome's naming of Hemileia vastatrix that year, with the point that those ridges are the film's own; the replacement crop reached by elimination through cinchona; the first commercial tea planting attributed to James Taylor at Loolecondera with the year and the acreage left in dispute as the sources leave them; the first Colombo auction of 30 July 1883; this eastern country's late and largely coffee-free arrival into planting, some of it onto upland grassland; the land ordinances recorded as law; and the district's flavour and price shown to be held in institutions rather than in leaf — a legally restricted region name, its own lines in the weekly auction quotations, and its weather printed beside its prices. The binding is reasoned from the two linked concepts as they already stand: feeling as the tasting of an object's flavour, in the everyday world of sights, tastes and touches, and an industry that has built a whole apparatus around a taste none of it holds. No citations were added. logline, two_layers, sequence and concept_merge are untouched — research contradicted nothing in them. best_time was rewritten because it is the film's central production fact and the research changed it: two clocks, a wind season from about June and a flavour season dated July–September with the finest usually put at end-July to mid-August, plus the separate fact that the leaf's price is set at auction weeks later, so the price beat cannot be shot in the same week as the pluck. why_here gained a history paragraph; what_to_film gained the rain-shadow frame across the crest, the grassland edge of the blocks, dated estate fabric and the printed market report; risks, unknowns, sources and research_note were extended; and images went from empty to five Commons files, each confirmed by title query before its URL was written. Guards held: no plantation labour history as decoration and nobody on an estate used to illustrate a colonial story, no remembrance or elegy for a planting era, colonial history recorded and never adjudicated, and no claim that anyone in the trade is greedy.

also_known_as.name: the eastern quality season

suggested_location.region: Badulla District, Uva Province, on the eastern slopes below the Namunukula range
suggested_location.why_here: This is the one kind of place where a taste is visibly manufactured by weather in front of the camera. For roughly six weeks from July the dry seasonal wind crosses this side of the range, rainfall drops away, days are hot and nights cold, and the leaf taken off these slopes acquires the character the trade prices separately from the rest of the year. That gives the film the shot it is built around, a wave of wind crossing a hillside seen from directly above, which is the concept stated rather than illustrated: the flavour is not in the leaf, it is what happens when conditions meet a mouth. It gives the second shot too, a bench of identical cups tasted and scored in seconds by somebody who registers nothing, which is the digest's point about a flat face and a delighted face both being accurate. And because the district is worked in small blocks feeding small factories rather than as one industrial site, the scale stays human and the whole cycle from bush to cup happens inside a few kilometres. Research has now put a history under it, which is what the record was missing. The industry that planted every acre in shot arrived because a different crop died: the coffee-leaf fungus whose first recorded specimens were sent down to the botanic gardens in May 1869 came off leaves from an estate on this same run of ridges, and within five years it was in every coffee district on the island. Quinine bark was tried next and failed to take over; tea, which had been in the island since the 1820s and 1830s without becoming a business, took the ground instead — and in this eastern country much of it went in for tea directly rather than onto dead coffee, because coffee had been slow to catch on this far from the capital, with some of the planting put on upland grassland the trade had taken to be not worth planting. The flavour and the price came afterwards, and both are now written into institutions that can be filmed: a region name that by law only leaf grown and made inside this boundary may carry, a separate line for this district's teas in every grade of the weekly auction quotations, and the district's weather printed in the same broker's report as the district's prices. That is the concept stated by the paperwork as well as by the wind: what all of it is built around is not held in the leaf or in anybody's mouth.

historical_thread.story:
The crop this district is planted with was chosen because a different crop died. Coffee was the British planters' crop in the island and it grew very fast: published figures give about 350 acres under coffee in 1834, some 79,000 acres by 1841, about 176,000 acres by 1869 and roughly 275,000 acres by 1880, with exports peaking around 1870 at a little over one million hundredweight. Then, in May 1869, George Henry Kendrick Thwaites, Director of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya, was sent specimens of diseased coffee leaves. His own account of it is flat and exact: 'This disease was first brought to my notice by some specimens of coffee leaves infected with it, which were sent to me from an estate in Madulsima.' Madulsima is on this side of the range — the Madulsima–Lunugala ridges run more than thirty kilometres north from Passara, so the first recorded leaves of the disease came off the same run of hills this film would be shot on. The fungus was described and named Hemileia vastatrix by the English mycologists Miles Joseph Berkeley and Christopher Edmund Broome in the Gardeners' Chronicle later that year, on Thwaites's Ceylon material; the type specimen is catalogued as Thwaites 834. Thwaites wrote afterwards that the speed of its spread through the coffee districts 'has been perfectly marvellous.' Within about five years every coffee district on the island was infected. Exports fell away through the 1870s and 1880s and by the end of the 1880s were under 100,000 hundredweight; something on the order of nine-tenths of the island's coffee was abandoned, and the accounts put the acreage that had to be stripped of dead coffee and replanted at more than 300,000 acres.

What replaced it was not settled in advance. Quinine bark was tried first: cinchona was grown experimentally at Hakgala from 1860 and commercially from 1873, rising from about 500 hectares in 1872 to some 6,000 by 1876, but it stayed a subsidiary planting inside the coffee and never took the industry over. Tea had been in the island for decades without becoming a business. Plants from China are reported to have been tried as early as 1824; in December 1839 seedlings from the Calcutta Botanic Gardens were under experiment at Peradeniya; and in September 1841 Maurice de Worms, with his brother Gabriel — nephews of the banker Nathan Mayer Rothschild — made a garden of Chinese cuttings at Condegalle near Pussellawa, brought a Chinese tea maker to manufacture it, and abandoned the attempt because the tea cost about five pounds sterling a pound and could not be sold. The planting the industry dates itself from is James Taylor's. Taylor, a Scot, had his first tea seed from Thwaites in 1860 and opened a clearing of about nineteen acres of Assam seed at Loolecondera, near Deltota south-east of Kandy, in 1867 — a coffee estate before it was a tea one. He withered the leaf by hand on the veranda of his bungalow and fired it over charcoal in a clay stove, and a purpose-built tea house followed on the estate in 1872. The first public tea auction in Colombo was held on 30 July 1883 at the premises of Somerville and Company under the auspices of the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce; one lot, of Kabaragala unassorted, sold at 45 cents a pound, the other four lots did not sell for want of bids, and auctions became regular from 1885.

This eastern country came into it late, and largely for tea rather than after coffee. Coffee was slow to catch on here although speculators had bought land: the province was far from Colombo and had no railway. The road to Haputale and Bandarawela was finished in 1866, the railway reached Bandarawela only in 1894 and Badulla in 1924, and Uva was constituted a province in February 1886. The estate registries, which cover 1870 to 1929 with gaps, date the ridge estates to that window — Mahadova 1870, Madulsima 1883 under the Madulsima Coffee and Cinchona Company, Passara Group 1898 — and name Bissett at Passara, Stewart at Yapame in the Lunugala country and Karslake at Madulsima. Henry Oswald Hoseason, who came out about 1874 and built the Demodera group to some four thousand acres, is credited with being the first planter to put tea on patana, the open upland grassland that had been taken to be not worth planting. So what the blocks here replaced was montane and submontane forest on the wet faces and patana on the dry ones. The land came from the Crown: under the Crown Lands (Encroachment) Ordinance No. 12 of 1840, reinforced by the Waste Lands Ordinance No. 1 of 1897, land that was forest, waste, unoccupied or uncultivated was presumed to be Crown land unless the contrary was proved, and Crown land was sold to planters.

The flavour and the price came after that, and both are now written into institutions. The wind is a known meteorological object: the kachchan, also called yal-hulang, is defined in the standard glossary as a hot dry west or south-west wind of föhn type in the lee of the hills during the south-west monsoon, well enough developed on the east coast to beat the sea breeze and push maximum temperatures towards 38 degrees. While the western slopes take the monsoon rain, these eastern slopes sit in its shadow and the air arrives dry, having dropped its water on the far side. The Sri Lanka Tea Board puts the eastern 'quality season' at July to September, the period of the south-west monsoon, notes that at this altitude the winds are usually dry, and describes the resulting tea as exotically aromatic and highly prized. The naming is legal: since 1975 the Board has controlled the use of the growing regions' names, and tea may carry this district's name only if it was both grown and made inside the region, which is defined for this district as 1,000 to 1,600 metres. The pricing is institutional too. The Colombo auction's weekly quotations carry 'Best Uvas' and 'Other Uvas' as their own lines, beside 'Best Westerns', 'Nuwara Eliyas' and the Uda Pussellawas, in each of the leaf grades; and the brokers print the week's weather for this region — sunny, bright, showers expected — on a page of the same report as the week's prices for it. A whole apparatus of law, category and weekly paperwork has been built around a taste that nothing in it holds.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C032's core sentence is that feeling is the tasting of an object's flavour, and that it comes in three ways — pleasant, painful, or neither — with no fourth way. C004 supplies the world that happens in: the everyday mind living among things seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched. The film already argues that this district is organised around a taste that is not stored anywhere. What the history adds is that the organising came second, and came by elimination. Nobody chose this crop for its taste in the first instance. A fungus removed the previous crop — and the first specimens of it anybody recorded came off leaves from these same ridges — and the industry then tried a bark for quinine, and then a leaf that had been sitting in the island unsold for a quarter of a century because it cost too much to make. Tea became the crop here because the alternative had died, and in this particular country much of the planting went in for tea directly rather than onto dead coffee, some of it on grassland the trade had thought worthless. That is the argument the film wants, put as events rather than as analogy: what the whole district exists to produce is not a thing that was wanted, but a flavour that turned out to be gettable here, in certain weeks, under a wind.

Then the machinery. The sources say the tasting happens when an object comes in front of a mind; they do not locate the flavour in the object and they do not locate it in the person. The history shows an industry that agrees with them in practice and has had to build around it: a region name restricted by law to leaf both grown and made inside a boundary, a separate line in an auction quotation for this district's teas in each grade, and a weather report for the district printed in the same document as the week's prices. None of that is holding a taste. It is holding the conditions under which one is expected to occur, which is what the sources say is all there is to hold. And the last movement is the sober one the digest is careful about: what feels good stands on conditions and hurts when they turn. The trade states that as a fact of business, not as a sermon — the wind gets up and drops daily, the season is a few weeks, some years it is poor — and the film lets the trade's flat version carry it. The history is not there to make anyone a culprit. An industry arrived because a crop died and it now turns a few weeks of weather into a price; that is recorded, and the film does not rule on it.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: That Thwaites, Director of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Peradeniya, recorded that the coffee-leaf disease was first brought to his notice by specimens of infected coffee leaves sent to him from an estate in Madulsima, and that the date given for this is May 1869. That the fungus was described and named Hemileia vastatrix by Berkeley and Broome in 1869 in the Gardeners' Chronicle from Thwaites's Ceylon material, and that a type specimen is catalogued as G. H. K. Thwaites 834. That the disease reached every coffee district on the island within about five years, that coffee exports peaked around 1870 and fell below 100,000 hundredweight by the end of the 1880s, and that the great majority of the island's coffee was abandoned. That published acreage figures for coffee run about 350 acres in 1834, 79,000 in 1841, 176,000 in 1869 and about 275,000 in 1880. That cinchona was grown experimentally at Hakgala from 1860 and commercially from 1873, and remained a subsidiary planting. That tea seedlings from the Calcutta Botanic Gardens were under experiment at Peradeniya in December 1839, and that Maurice and Gabriel de Worms, nephews of Nathan Mayer Rothschild, made a garden of Chinese cuttings at Condegalle, Pussellawa, from September 1841, employed a Chinese tea maker, and gave it up on cost. That James Taylor received his first tea seed from Thwaites in 1860, that he opened a clearing of Assam seed at Loolecondera near Deltota which had been a coffee estate, that he withered leaf on his bungalow veranda and fired it over charcoal, and that a tea house was built on the estate in 1872. That the first public Colombo tea auction was held on 30 July 1883 at Somerville and Company's premises under the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, that one lot of Kabaragala unassorted sold at 45 cents a pound while four lots went unsold, and that auctions became regular from 1885. That the Crown Lands (Encroachment) Ordinance No. 12 of 1840 and the Waste Lands Ordinance No. 1 of 1897 presumed forest, waste, unoccupied or uncultivated land to be Crown land unless the contrary was proved. That Uva was constituted a province in February 1886, that the road to Haputale and Bandarawela was completed in 1866, and that the railway reached Bandarawela in 1894 and Badulla in 1924. That the Madulsima–Lunugala ridges run more than thirty kilometres north from Passara, that the main ridge between them stands at roughly 1,200 to 1,300 metres, and that the range's main peak, Namunukula, is 2,036 metres. That the kachchan, also called yal-hulang, is defined in the standard meteorological glossary as a hot dry west or south-west wind of föhn type in the lee of these hills during the south-west monsoon, and that it is strong enough on the east coast to overcome the sea breeze and bring maximum temperatures near 38 degrees. That the Sri Lanka Tea Board dates the eastern quality season to July–September, the period of the south-west monsoon, and states that at this altitude the winds are usually dry, having shed their moisture on the hills below. That the Board has controlled the use of the growing regions' names since 1975 and requires tea bearing this district's name to have been grown and manufactured within it, at 1,000 to 1,600 metres. That the Colombo auction's weekly quotations list this district's teas as their own lines in each grade alongside the other high-grown districts, and that the brokers publish the district's weekly weather in the same report as its prices: in the sale of 9 and 10 September 2025, for example, Best Uvas in the Pekoe/FBOP line were quoted at Rs. 1,420–1,950 a kilo against Rs. 1,300–1,850 for Best Westerns, while in the BOP line Best Uvas at Rs. 1,300–1,340 stood below Best Westerns at Rs. 1,340–1,480.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed:
The first planting's date and size. Most accounts give 1867 and nineteen acres. One industry history argues the year 'could perhaps be correctly taken as 1866/67 as planting may have commenced late in '66 and ended in early '67 along with the North East Monsoon rains'. The Sri Lanka Tea Board's own page says Taylor withered the first leaves in 1866 and gives twenty acres. All three readings are kept.

Who was first. Loolecondera is named as the first commercial tea planting; Rothschild estate at Pussellawa and the Condagalla division at Ramboda are named as the first tea *experiments*, from 1841, and partisans of the de Worms brothers press their priority. The usual reconciliation is experimental against commercial scale, after about twenty-eight years of trial plots from 1839. There is a further, separate claim about first manufacture: W. J. Jenkins of Condagalla claimed to have carried out the first experiments in making tea, and Taylor claimed it too.

The twenty-three pounds. The version in general circulation is that twenty-three pounds of Loolecondera tea reached London in 1873. One industry history instead records 'a valuation of 23 lbs of Loolecondra tea at three shillings per pound by a valuer in Mincing Lane' in 1881, and puts Ceylon teas' appearance in the London market in 1878 and in Melbourne in 1880. The Tea Board attaches twenty-three pounds to Taylor's first consignment without a year. These cannot all be right and the film does not average them.

Where the disease was first seen. The primary trace is Thwaites's own wording, 'an estate in Madulsima'. The naming of Galloola estate and of a superintendent, Donald Reid, appears in later secondary accounts and could not be carried back to a contemporary source from here. One published account also describes Madulsima as 'a newly-opened coffee district in the south-west of Ceylon', which does not fit the district's position on the eastern slopes; whether the estate in question lies inside the ridges this film covers is therefore unresolved.

The wind's direction and origin. The meteorological definition is a west or south-west föhn wind belonging to the south-west monsoon. Trade writing variously calls it a wind that 'blows in from the Northwest of the island, originating in the Bay of Bengal', attributes the July–August quality season to 'the northeast monsoon's dry winds', and describes it as 'a drying cool wind coming in from the north or east of the ocean'. The monsoon named in most of the trade versions is the wrong one for July and August, and the film follows the meteorological definition while recording that the trade's own account of its own wind is inconsistent. The spelling varies: kachchan, kacchan, cachan.

When the season is, and how reliably. The glossary puts the wind at June and July; the Tea Board puts the quality season at July to September; trade writing gives 'end July to mid-August' for the finest, 'June to September' for the district's exclusive quality teas, and 'occasionally into early September'. No source found gives a year-by-year record of when the season arrived or failed, so its reliability is not established.

The price premium. That this district's character is 'highly prized by trade and connoisseur alike' is the Tea Board's own unquantified wording; that its teas 'command the highest prices' is trade writing. What is documented is narrower and different in kind: the auction quotes the district separately in every grade, and in season its flavoury leafy grades quote above the western high growns while its BOP can quote below them in the same week. The all-time record prices reported for a high-grown estate in this district — Rs. 2,600 a kilo for an FBOP, beating that estate's own record of Rs. 2,250 set a week earlier — were set at the sale of 3 May 2022, outside the July–September season altogether. A 2026 study of 105 weekly broker reports covering November 2023 to March 2026 found that weather histories gave only limited, catalogue-specific predictive information about prices, and it reports no seasonal analysis for this district at all. So: the district's separate identity and separate pricing are documented; a standing district-wide premium, and a measurable seasonal premium over the district's own off-season, are not established from any series found here.

The chemistry of the flavour. The mentholated or wintergreen note is widely attributed to methyl salicylate produced by the bush under drought stress. That attribution is repeated across trade writing; no peer-reviewed measurement of this district's seasonal tea specifically was found, and the general research consulted concerns drought effects on tea volatiles rather than this season.

The estate dates. Mahadova 1870, Madulsima 1883, Passara Group 1898 come from a registry which states that its estate and planter data covers only 1870 to 1929, with gaps. Those are recorded ownership dates and are not evidence of when the ground was first cleared. The figures sometimes quoted for forest conversion — 26 per cent of montane and 53 per cent of submontane forest under coffee by 1880 — appear in secondary summaries and were not checked against the paper they come from; they are island-wide in any case and not specific to this district.

what_to_film: The district from the air at first light: one crop to the skyline, cloud pouring over the ridge and down the eastern face, and burning off.
The wind itself from directly above, crossing the bush as a moving wave, with the colour of the slope changing as it passes. This is the payoff shot and everything else is built around getting it.
The pluck at working speed, at waist height and close, in the heat, without commentary.
The afternoon weigh-in: the hook, the tally, and the talk and laughing in the queue, kept in the same sequence as the heat of the pluck.
The factory through the night: withering troughs with the fans on, the rollers, the firing, and the smell changing as the hours pass, filmed as light and machinery rather than as a process explainer.
The tasting bench in flat daylight: the rows of identical cups, the pour, the spoon going down the line, the spit, the number written.
Grading, stencilling and loading, and a price being said out loud in the yard with the wind still in the trees.
The same hillside after the wind has dropped, in ordinary weather, with the bench empty and the cups upside down. This is beat 7 and the film ends on it.

From the air along the crest in the season: cloud and rain standing on the far side of the ridge and hard dry light on this side of it, in one frame. That is the rain shadow, which is the whole mechanism, and it is the history and the flavour in the same shot.

The upper edge of the planted blocks, where tea stops and open upland grassland begins — the ground the trade held to be not worth planting until the 1870s and 1880s, and the reason some of this country was planted straight to tea.
Estate fabric that carries its own date on its face: cast-iron machinery plates, a factory datestone, a weighing hook, a boundary marker. Filmed as objects, with nobody working them in frame.
A broker's printed weekly market report, open at the page where this district's week of weather is set beside this district's week of prices. Filmed as a document, close, in flat light.
suggested_location.access: By road from Badulla, roughly eighteen kilometres along the highway that runs on towards the east coast; the district is a working landscape of estates, smallholdings and factories rather than a site with a gate. Access is plot by plot and factory by factory, through estate managements and, separately, through the people who would actually be filmed. Tasting rooms are ordinary working rooms and are not normally open to visitors. Nothing in the film requires access to a visitor-facing factory tour, which is a different kind of place from the one this film wants.
suggested_location.best_time: This is the film's central production fact and there are two clocks, which do not run together. The wind: the kachchan is a föhn wind belonging to the south-west monsoon, and the meteorological definition puts it over these lee slopes from about June, with the standard glossary naming June and July and the trade naming June to September. The flavour: the trade's eastern quality season is dated by the Tea Board to July–September, and the finest leaf is most often put at the end of July to the middle of August, sometimes running into early September. So the plan is a block of about four weeks from mid-July with the option to extend into the third week of September — and inside that block the payoff shot is a day-by-day gamble, because the wind gets up in the late morning and drops at dusk and there are days in the season when it does not blow at all. No year-by-year record of when the season arrived or failed was found, so no reliability figure can be given and the only prudent assumption is that in some years it will not come. The price beat cannot be shot in the same week as the pluck: leaf made in the season reaches the Colombo sale weeks later, so the graded sacks, the figure said out loud and the printed market report belong to late August and September, not to the week the wind was filmed. Within the day: first light on the eastern face for cloud pouring over the crest and for the first leaf off the bush; late morning to late afternoon for the wind at strength; flat daylight for the tasting bench, which is when it is genuinely used. The closing beat needs a second, much shorter visit outside the season, because the film ends on the same hillside in ordinary weather with the cups upside down.

suggested_location.research_note:
Two passes. The first (2026-09-21) established the seasonal window, the dry wind and its effect on flavour, the elevation band, the position of Passara and Lunugala on the eastern slopes of the range, and the coordinates of the town, from the trade sources listed. The second (2026-09-26) added the historical thread and is desk research throughout.

What the second pass established. The coffee collapse and the switch are documented to a primary trace: Thwaites's own statement that the disease was first brought to his notice by specimens sent from an estate in Madulsima, dated May 1869, and Berkeley and Broome's naming of Hemileia vastatrix that year from his material, with a type specimen catalogued under his name. Madulsima lies on the same run of ridges as the film's district, which is the fact the thread turns on. The first commercial tea planting is attributed to James Taylor at Loolecondera on the authority of the industry's own histories and the Tea Board, and those same sources disagree about the year (1867, or 1866/67, or 1866) and the acreage (nineteen or twenty). The famous '23 lb to London in 1873' does not survive contact with the industry's own record, which puts a Mincing Lane valuation of 23 lb at three shillings a pound in 1881 and Ceylon tea's appearance in the London market in 1878; the variants are kept apart in the thread and not averaged. The wind is the best-founded item: it has a formal meteorological definition as a south-west-monsoon föhn wind in the lee of the hills, and the trade's own descriptions of it contradict both that definition and each other, several of them naming the wrong monsoon. The district's separate identity and separate pricing are documented institutionally — a legally controlled region name since 1975, a defined 1,000–1,600 m band, and its own lines in the weekly auction quotations alongside the district's own weather report — and one week's quotations were read directly from a broker's report to check the premium claim rather than repeat it.

What could not be verified. The naming of Galloola estate and of a superintendent as the first observers is secondary and was not traced to a contemporary source, so whether the first recorded leaves came from inside the film's own ridges is unresolved. Estate registry dates cover only 1870–1929 with gaps and record ownership rather than first clearing. No year-by-year series of the season's arrival or failure was found, and no published series shows a measurable seasonal price premium for the district over its own off-season; the record prices reported for a high-grown estate here were set in May, outside the season. The methyl-salicylate explanation of the flavour is repeated everywhere and was not found measured for this district's seasonal tea. Which particular estates and factories catch the wind, whether any factory would allow night filming or filming at the tasting bench, whether a broker's report may be filmed and on whose permission, current access and permissions, drone rules over estate land, and the pay and conditions of the crews all remain unverified.

Deliberately excluded. The plantation labour history of this country is real and is not this film's subject; it is not narrated, and no person on an estate is used to illustrate a colonial story. The district's pre-plantation history includes the 1817–18 rebellion in this province and its suppression, which the research surfaced and which this film does not enter. The land ordinances are recorded as law, and nothing in the thread is adjudicated, denounced, admired or mourned.

Images. The first pass left the images array empty because no candidate URL could be confirmed from a rate-limited machine. Five Wikimedia Commons files have now been found through the search API and each confirmed individually by title query before its URL was written: two tea-country views inside the district (one at Passara, one at Lunugala), a hill above the town whose own file coordinates match the point this record proposes, a view of the range itself, and one upland viewpoint in the same country. Commons holds nothing usable for the working interiors the film is built on — no tasting bench, no withering loft, no factory in this district — and the captions say what each picture is and is not.

unknowns: No estate, factory or crew has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
Whether a working tasting bench can be filmed at all, and on whose permission, is unverified.
How reliably the seasonal wind arrives in any given year, and how visible it is on the slope from the air, has not been checked on the ground.
Whether the wind crossing the bush is visible from the air in the way the film is built around was not established; no published photograph or footage confirming it was found.
No year-by-year record of the season's arrival or failure was found, so the shoot cannot be planned against a known probability.
Whether the estate on which the coffee disease was first recorded can be named from a contemporary source, and whether it lies within the ridges this film covers, is unresolved.
Whether a broker's printed weekly market report may be filmed, and on whose permission, is unverified.
